summary: Welcome to Laika Program! For the Space Mission Design Game Challenge, we built a zero-install, 8-bit browser game. Players act as Flight Director alongside Laika, leading a crew of 17 animal astronauts inspired by the real animals who pioneered spaceflight, to design, launch, and operate a NASA space mission. The playable mission recreates STS-125, Hubble's final servicing mission, and follows the real engineering cycle: build a spacecraft within rocket mass and solar power limits; match crew skills to mission roles; pilot a multi-stage ascent through Max Q; manage hardware failures and crises in orbit; and complete five minigames based on real Atlantis EVA tasks. A graded final report explains why the mission succeeded or failed, compares it to the real NASA mission, and invites players to redesign and relaunch.  Spacecraft systems engineering is usually hidden behind technical tools that keep newcomers out. Laika Program turns its trade-offs into visual gauges and quick decisions, grounded in NASA open data and public-domain mission photography. With a real-time English-Spanish language selector switch and no installs or accounts, it brings mission design to classrooms, families, and Spanish-speaking audiences.
details:
SpaceTaco's Project Solution

Laika Program is a zero-install, 8-bit browser game that teaches spacecraft systems engineering by having the player run a real NASA mission. As Flight Director and with the guidance of Laika, the player leads 17 cartoon animal astronauts inspired by the real animals who pioneered spaceflight, including Belka, Strelka, Ham, Félicette and Miss Baker. Together they recreate STS-125 (May 2009), the last time astronauts visited the Hubble Space Telescope. Our answer to the Space Mission Design Game challenge is to make players think like mission engineers: every kilogram, watt and crew choice affects the rest of the mission.

How Does Our Solution Work

Each mission follows the engineering cycle real teams use:

  1. Design (Hangar): The player builds the spacecraft from six part categories: structure, propulsion, solar power, communications, shielding and instruments. Four internal systems configure themselves. There is no money budget. Instead the player faces the trade-offs engineers face: staying under the rocket's mass limit, generating enough power, meeting the destination's propulsion and shielding minimums, and fitting an antenna strong enough to send the science data home.
  2. Crew: The player fills each seat (Commander, Pilot, Mission Specialist) by comparing skill bars (Speed, Analysis, Tech, Calm), short bios and a team radar chart.
  3. Launch: A one-button ascent where design choices matter. A heavier ship narrows the safe throttle zone through Max Q and climbs more slowly, and a stronger engine widens the orbital burn window.
  4. Operations: In orbit, the player fixes 10 types of hardware failure through quick one-button repairs. The player also handles crises by matching crew skills to each problem while managing fatigue, blackouts and communication loss. Five minigames recreate the real Atlantis tasks: grabbing Hubble with the robotic arm, installing the Wide Field Camera 3, replacing gyroscopes and batteries, repairing the STIS spectrograph (111 screws), and releasing Hubble before landing at Edwards Air Force Base.
  5. Debrief: An A–F report scores objectives, science, ship integrity and crisis handling. It explains the root cause of each failure, compares the player's run with the real mission, and invites the player to Redesign & Relaunch.

The Game Benefits

  • Easy to start: Visual gauges and quick decisions replace technical tools, so a 10-year-old and a parent can play together.
  • Learning through failure: The redesign-and-relaunch loop teaches the trial-and-error at the heart of systems engineering. Mistakes become lessons, not game-overs.
  • Grounded in reality: The game uses NASA open data, the real STS-125 crew and tasks, and public-domain photos from the NASA Image and Video Library.
  • Inclusive: A live EN | ES switch covers the whole game, including the minigames, so it also reaches Spanish-speaking audiences.
  • Zero install: It runs in any modern browser with no accounts and no downloads, which makes it ready for classrooms.

Our Goal

We want students, families and the general public to come away understanding that a spacecraft is a set of compromises, and that real missions succeed through careful design, teamwork and learning from failure. We also want to honor the animal pioneers who made human spaceflight possible. Next we plan to add an Artemis lunar south pole mission and a crewed mission to Mars, both already designed in the game's data.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript.
  • All missions, rockets, parts, crew and events are stored as editable JSON data files.
  • Game logic is kept separate from the display code.
  • 16-color PICO-8 palette on a pixelated canvas. The crew portraits are drawn as vector art and turned into 40×40 pixel sprites when the game starts.
  • Chiptune sound effects made in the browser with the Web Audio API.
  • Open-source fonts (Press Start 2P, VT323) and icons (Pixelarticons).
  • A Node.js balance simulator that plays hundreds of automated missions to tune difficulty.
